title: Theorem
body_md: Suppose that $T$ is a theory in a fragment of $\mathbb{L}_{\kappa, \aleph_{0}}$ where $\kappa$ is a measurable cardinal.  If $T$ is categorical in the cardinal $\lambda > \kappa + | T | $, then  ${\mathcal K}_{< \lambda}$, the class of models of $T$ of power strictly less than $\lambda$ (but $\geq \chi = \kappa+ |T|$), has the amalgamation property (see Definition \ref{X1.3} (1)(2)).

label: a2
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{a2}\ 

    (1) For cardinals $\kappa \le \lambda, \  \mathbb{L}_{ \lambda, \kappa}$ is the logic such that for any vocabulary $\tau,$ $\mathbb{L}_{\lambda, \kappa}(\tau)$ is the smallest set of (possibly infinitary) formulas in the vocabulary $\tau$ which contains all first-order formulas and which is closed under: 

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(A)] the formation of conjunctions (disjunctions) of any set of formulas of power less than $\lambda$, provided that the set of free variables in the conjunctions (disjunctions) has power less than $\kappa$,

        \item[(B)] the formation of $\forall \bar x \varphi,  \exists \bar x \varphi$, where $\bar x = \langle x_\alpha \colon \alpha < \alpha_{\ast} \rangle$ is a sequence of variables of length $\alpha_{\ast} < \kappa$. 
    \end{enumerate}

    (2) Whenever we use the notation $\varphi(\bar{x})$ to denote a formula in $\mathbb{L}_{\lambda, \kappa},$ we mean that $\bar{x}$ is a sequence $\langle x_{\alpha} \colon \alpha < \alpha_{\ast} \rangle$ as above. So if $\varphi(\bar{x})$ is a formula in $\mathbb{L}_{\kappa, \aleph_{0}},$ then $\bar{x}$ is a finite sequence of variables. 

    (3) So $\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{L}_{\aleph_{0}, \aleph_{0}}$ is a first order logic.

label: a8
title: Notation
body_md:
\label{a8}\ 

    (1) $\mathcal F$ denotes a fragment of $\mathbb{L}_{\kappa, \aleph_{0}}(\tau)$, i.e. a set of formulas of $\mathbb{L}_{\kappa, \aleph_{0}}(\tau)$ which contains all atomic formulas of $\tau$, and which is closed under negations, finite conjunctions (finite disjunctions), and the formation of subformulas.  An $\mathcal F$-formula is just an element of $\mathcal F$.
    
    (2) $T$ is a theory in $\mathbb{L}_{\kappa, \aleph_{0}}(\tau)$, so there is a fragment $\mathcal F$ of $\mathbb{L}_{\kappa, \aleph_{0}}$ such that $T \subseteq \mathcal F$ and $| \mathcal F | < | T|^+ + \kappa$. Let $\mathcal{F}_{T}$ be the minimal such $\mathcal{F}$. If not said otherwise, $T$ and $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{F}_{T}$ are fixed. 
        
    (3) Models of $T$ (invariably referred to as models) are $\tau$-structures which satisfy the sentences of $T$. They are generally denoted $M, N, \dots, $ and $  |M|$ is the universe of the $\tau$-structure $M; \; \Vert M \Vert$ is the cardinality of $|M|$.
    
    (4) For a set $A, \; |A|$ is the cardinality of $A$ and $^{< \omega} A$ is the set of finite sequences in $A$ and for $\bar a = \langle a_0 \dots a_{n-1} \rangle \in \; ^{< \omega} A, \ \rm{lg} (\bar a) = n$ is the length of $\bar a$. Similarly, if $\bar a=\langle a_\zeta:\zeta<\delta\rangle$, we write $\lg(\bar a)=\delta$, where $\delta$ is an ordinal.
    
    (5) For an element $R$ of $\tau$ and a $\tau$-model $M$, let $\mathrm{val}(M, R)$, or $R^M$, be the interpretation of $R$ in the $\tau$-structure $M$.
        
    (6) We ignore models of power less than $\kappa$.  $K$ is the class of all models of $T$; $$ K_\lambda = \{ M \in K: || M || = \lambda \}, \;  K_{< \lambda} = \underset{\mu < \lambda} \bigcup K_\mu, \; K_{\le \lambda} = \underset{\mu \le \lambda} \bigcup K_\mu, \, K_{[\mu, \lambda)} = \underset{\mu \le \chi< \lambda} \bigcup K_\chi. $$
        
    (7) We write $f  \colon M \underset{\mathcal F} \rightarrow N$ (may be abbreviated $f: M \rightarrow N$) to mean
    that $f$ is an $\mathcal F$-elementary embedding (briefly, an embedding) of $M$ into $N$,  i.e. $f$ is a function with domain $|M|$ into $|N|$ such that for every $\mathcal F$-formula $\varphi (\bar x)$, and $\bar a \in \; ^{< \omega} |M|$ with $\lg(\bar a) = \lg (\bar x),  M \vDash \varphi [\bar a]$ iff $N \vDash \varphi [f (\bar a)]$, where if $\bar a = \langle a_i: i < n \rangle$, then $f (\bar a) := \langle f (a_i): i < n \rangle$.
    
    (8) In the special case where an embedding $f$ is a set-inclusion (so that $|M| \subseteq  \vert N \vert$), we write $M \prec_{\mathcal F} N$ (briefly $M \prec N$), instead of $f: M \underset{\mathcal F} \rightarrow N.$ We may say that $M$ is an $\mathcal F$-elementary sub-model of $N$, or $N$ is an $\mathcal F$-elementary extension of $M$.

label: a11
title: Notation
body_md:
\label{a11}\ 

    (1) $(I, \le_I), (J, \le_J)$ are partial orders; we will not bother to subscript the order relation unless really necessary; we may write $I$ for $(I, \le).$ We say $(I, \le)$ is directed iff for every $i_1$ and $i_2$ in $I$, there is $i \in I$ such that $i_1 \le i$ and $i_2 \le i$. $(I, <)^\ast$ is the (reverse) partial order $(I^\ast, <^\ast)$ where $I^\ast = I$ and $s <^\ast t$ iff $t < s$.
        
    (2) A sequence $\langle M_i: i \in I \rangle$ of models indexed by $I$ is a $\prec_{\mathcal F}$-directed system iff $(I, \le)$ is a directed partial order and for $i \le j$  in $I, M_i \prec_{\mathcal F} M_j$.

    Note that, the union $\underset{i \in I} \cup M_i$ of a $\prec_{\mathcal F}$-directed system $\langle M_i  \colon i \in I \rangle$ of $\tau$-structures is an $\tau$-structure. In fact, more is true.
head: environment

label: X1.1
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{X1.1}\  

    (1) (Tarski-Vaught property) The union of a $\prec_{\mathcal F}$-directed system $\langle M_i : i \in I \rangle$ of models of $T$ is a model of $T$, and for every $j \in I, M_j \prec_{\mathcal F} \underset{i \in I} \cup M_i$.
    
    (2) For $\bar{M}$ as above, if $M$ is a fixed model of $T$ such that for every $i \in I$ there is $f_i \colon M_i \underset{\mathcal F} \rightarrow M,$ $I$ is directed, and for all $i \le j$ in $I, f_i \subseteq f_j$, then $\underset{i \in I} \cup f_i: \underset{i \in I} \cup M_i \underset{\mathcal F} \rightarrow M$. In particular, if $M_i \prec_{\mathcal F} M$ and $f_{i}$ is the identity function on $M_{i}$ for every $i \in I$, then $\underset{i \in I}  \cup M_i \prec_{\mathcal F} M$. Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal.  A $\prec_{\mathcal F}$-chain of models of length $\alpha$ is a sequence $\langle M_\beta: \beta < \alpha \rangle$ of models such that if $\beta < \gamma < \alpha$, then $M_\beta \prec_{\mathcal F} M_\gamma$.  The chain is continuous if for every limit ordinal $\beta < \alpha,  M_\beta = \underset{\gamma < \beta}  \cup M_\gamma$.

label: X1.2
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{X1.2}\      
    
    (1) (Downward L\"owenheim-Skolem Property):
    Suppose that $M$ is a model of $T$, $ A \subseteq | M |$ and $\max (\kappa + | T |, |A| ) \le \lambda \le || M ||$.  \underline{Then} there is a model $N$ such that $A \subseteq | N |,  || N || = \lambda$ and $N \prec_{\mathcal{F}} M$.
    
    (2) If $N$ and $M_{1} \subseteq M_{2}$ are $\tau$-models, $\mathcal{F}$ is a fragment of $\mathbb{L}_{\kappa, \aleph_{0}},$ and $M_{\ell} \prec_{\mathcal{F}} N$ for $\ell = 1, 2$ \underline{then} $M_{1} \prec_{\mathcal{F}} M_{2}.$

label: X1.3
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{X1.3}\ 

    (1) Suppose that $<$ is a binary relation on a class $K$ of models (mainly $(K, <) = (K_{\mathfrak{k}}, <_{\mathfrak{k}}$), see below). We say $\mathcal K = \langle K, < \rangle$ has the \emph{amalgamation property} (AP) \underline{iff} for every $M, M_1, M_2 \in K$, if $f_i$ is an isomorphism from $M$ onto $\mathrm{rng}(f_i)$ and $\mathrm{rng}(f_i)<M_i$ for $i=1,2$, then there exist $N\in K$ and isomorphisms $g_i$ from $M_i$ onto $\mathrm{rng}(g_i)$ for $i = 1,2$ such that $\mathrm{rng}(g_i) < N$ and $g_1 f_1 = g_2 f_2$. The model $N$ is called an \emph{amalgam} of $M_1, M_2$ over $M$ with respect to $f_1, f_2$.
    
    (2) An $\tau$-structure $M$ is an \emph{amalgamation base} (a.b.) for $\mathcal K = \langle K, < \rangle$ iff $M \in K$ and whenever for $i = 1, 2, M_i \in K$ and $f_i$ is an isomorphism from $M$ onto $\mathrm{rng}(f_i), \, \mathrm{rng}(f_i) < M_i$, then there exist $N \in K$ and isomorphisms $g_i \ (i = 1,2)$ from $M_i$ onto $\mathrm{rng}(g_i)$ such that $\mathrm{rng}(g_i) < N$ and $g_1 f_1 = g_2 f_2$.

    (3) We say  $\mathcal K = \langle K, < \rangle$ has AP iff every model in $K$ is an a.b. for $\mathcal K$.
head: environment

label: X1.3A
title: Example
body_md:
\label{X1.3A}
    Suppose that $T$ is a theory in first-order logic having an infinite  model.  Define, for $M, N$ in the class $K_{\le | T| + \aleph_0}$ of models of $T$ of power at most $|T|+\aleph_0$, $M < N$ iff  the indentity on $\vert M \vert$ is an embedding of $M$ onto an elementary sub-model of $N.$   Then $\mathcal K_{\le |T| + \aleph_0} = \langle K_{\le |T| + \aleph_0}, < \rangle$ has AP, (see \cite{CK73}).
head: environment

label: X1.3B
title: Example
body_md:
\label{X1.3B}
    Suppose that $T$ is a theory in $\mathbb{L}_{\kappa, \aleph_{0}}$ and $\mathcal F$ is  a fragment of $\mathbb{L}_{\kappa, \aleph_{0}}$ containing $T$ with $| \mathcal F| < |T|^+ + \kappa$. Let $<$ be the binary relation $\prec_{\mathcal F}$ defined on the class $K$ of all models of $T$.  $M \in K$ is an a.b. for $\mathcal K$ iff whenever for $i = 1, 2, M_i \in K$ and $f_i$ is an $\prec_{\mathcal F}$-elementary embedding of $M$ into $M_i$, there exist $N \in K$ and $\mathcal F$-elementary embeddings $g_i (i = 1,2)$ of $M_i$ into $N$ such that $g_1 f_1 = g_2 f_2$.

label: u2
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{u2}
    We say $\mathfrak{k} = (K_{\mathfrak{k}}, \leq_{\mathfrak{k}})$ is an a.e.c. with 
    L.S.T. number $\lambda(\mathfrak{k}) = \mathrm{LS}_{\mathfrak{k}} = \mathrm{LST}(\mathfrak{k})$, we may write $K$ for $K_{\mathfrak{k}},$ \underline{when} $K$ is a class of $\tau_{\mathfrak{k}}$-models, $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$ a two-place relation on $K$ and 

    \begin{itemize}
        \item     \underline{Ax 0}:  The holding of $M \in K,N \le_\mathfrak{k} M$  depend on $N,M$ only up to isomorphism, i.e. $[M \in K,M \cong N \Rightarrow N \in K]$ and 
        [if $N \le_\mathfrak{k} M$ and $f$ is an isomorphism from $M$ onto the $\tau$-model $M'$ and $ f \, \restriction \,  N$ is an isomorphism from $N$ onto $N'$ \underline{then} $N' \le_\mathfrak{k} M'$.]

        \item     \underline{Ax I}:  if $M \le_{\mathfrak{k}} N$  then $M \subseteq N$ (i.e. $M$ is a sub-model of $N$).

        \item     \underline{Ax II}:  $M_0 \le_{\mathfrak{k}} M_1 \le_{\mathfrak{k}} M_2$ implies $M_0 \le_{\mathfrak{k}} M_2$ and $M \le_{\mathfrak{k}} M$ for $M \in K$.

        \item     \underline{Ax III}:  If $\lambda$ is a regular cardinal, $M_i \ (i < \lambda)$ is a $\le_{\mathfrak{k}}$-increasing (i.e. $i < j < \lambda$ implies  $M_i \le_\mathfrak{k} M_j$) and continuous (i.e. for every limit ordinal $\delta < \lambda,M_\delta = \bigcup_{i < \delta} M_i$) \underline{then} $M_0 \le_{\mathfrak{k}} \bigcup_{i < \lambda} M_i$. Hence $M_{j} \leq_{\kappa} \bigcup_{i < \lambda} M_{i}$ for every $j < \lambda.$  

        \item     \underline{Ax IV}:  If $\lambda$ is a regular cardinal and $M_i$  (for $i < \lambda)$ is $\le_\mathfrak{k}$-increasing continuous and $M_i \le_\mathfrak{k} N$ for $i < \lambda$ 
        \underline{then}  $\bigcup_{i < \lambda} M_i \le_{\mathfrak{k}} N$.

        \item     \underline{Ax V}:  If $N_0 \subseteq N_1 \le_\mathfrak{k} M$ and $N_0 \le_{\mathfrak{k}} M$  \underline{then} $N_0 \le_\mathfrak{k} N_1$.

        \item     \underline{Ax VI}:  If $A \subseteq N \in K$ and $|A| \le \text{ LST}(\mathfrak{k})$  then for some $M \le_\mathfrak{k} N,A \subseteq |M|$ and $\|M\| \le  \text{ LST}(\mathfrak{k})$ (and $\text{\rm LST}(\mathfrak{k})$ is the minimal infinite cardinal satisfying this axiom which is $\ge |\tau|$;  the $\ge |\tau|$ is for notational simplicity). 
    \end{itemize}

\label{w2}
    Suppose that $M$ is an $\tau$-structure, $I$ is a non-empty set, $D$ is an ultra-filter on $I$ (but see Definition \ref{w5}(5)), and $G$ is a filter on $I \times I$.
    
    (1) For each $g \in {}^{I}|M|$, let
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] $\mathrm{eq}(g) \coloneqq \{ \langle i, j \rangle \in I \times I \colon g (i) = g (j) \},$ and

        \item[(b)] $g / D \coloneqq \{ f \in {}^I |M| \colon g = f \,  \operatorname{Mod} \, D \}$ where, $$g = f \; \operatorname{Mod} \; D \text{ iff }\{ i \in I \colon g (i) = f (i) \} \in D.$$ 
    \end{enumerate}
    
    (2) Let $\underset{D / G} \Pi |M| \coloneqq \{ g / D \colon  g \in {}^I |M|$ and $\mathrm{eq} (g) \in G  \}$. Note that $\underset{D / G} \Pi |M|$ is a non-empty subset of $\Pi_D |M| = \{ g / D  \colon g \in {}^I|M| \}$ and is closed under the constants and functions of the ultra-power $\Pi_D M$ of $M$ modulo $D$. 
    
    (3) The limit ultra-power $\underset{D/G}  \Pi M$ of the $\tau$-structure $M$ (with respect to ($I, D, G$)) is the substructure of $\Pi_D M$ whose universe is the set $\underset{D / G} \Pi |M|$.  The canonical map $d$ from $M$ into $\underset{D / G} \Pi M$ is defined by $d (a) = \langle a_i : i \in I \rangle / D$, where $a_i = a$ for every $i \in I$.  
    
    (4) Note that the limit ultra-power $\underset {D / G}  \Pi M$ depends only on the equivalence relations which are
    in $G$, i.e. if {\bf E} is the set of all equivalence relations on $I$ and $G
    \cap$ {\bf E} $= G' \cap$ {\bf E}, where $G'$ is a filter on $I \times I$, then $\underset
    {D / G}  \Pi M = \underset{D / G'}  \Pi M$.

    (1) Let $E = \underset{y \in Y}{\Pi} D_y $ be the set of $ s \subseteq I$ such that there are $y_1 < \dots < y_n$ in $Y$ satisfying:
    
    \begin{enumerate}

body_md:
et us list some general facts which facilitate the proof.
    
    Fact (A): Let $\underline{\kappa}$ denote the linear order $(\kappa,<)$ where $<$ is the usual order $\in \upharpoonright \kappa \times\kappa$. If $J_1=\underline\kappa+J_0$, then $\underline\kappa {\underset{\text{nice}}  \subseteq} J_1$
    ($+$ is the addition of linear orders in which all elements in the first order
    precede those in the second).
    
    Fact (B): If $\underline\kappa \subseteq (I,<)$, $\underline\kappa$ is unbounded in $(I,<)$ and
    $J_1=I+J_0$, then $I\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq J_1$.
    
    Fact (C): If $I\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq J$, then $I+J_1\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq J+J_1$.
    
    Fact (D): $I\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq J$ iff $(J<)^*\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq (I,<)^*$.
    
    Fact (E): If $\langle I_{\alpha} \colon\alpha \le \delta\rangle$ is a continuous increasing
    sequence of linear
    orders and for $\alpha<\delta$, $I_{\alpha}\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq I_{\alpha +1}$, then
    $I_\alpha\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq I_{\delta}$.
    
    Now using these facts, let us prove the criterion. Define an equivalence
    relation $E$
    on $J\setminus I$ as follows: $tEs$ iff $t$ and $s$ define the
    same Dedekind cut
    in $(I,<)$. Let $\{ t_{\alpha} \colon  \alpha<\delta \} $ be a set of representatives of
    the $E$-equivalence
    classes. For each $\beta \le \delta$, define
    $$I_{\beta}=J\upharpoonright \left \{ t \colon t\in I \vee {\underset{{\alpha<\beta}} \bigvee} tEt_{\alpha} \right \}$$
    so $I_0=I$, $I_{\delta}=J$ and $\langle I_{\alpha} \colon\alpha \le \delta\rangle$ is a
    continuous increasing sequence of linear orders.
    By Fact (E), to show that $I \underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq J$,
    it suffices to show that $I_{\alpha}\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq I_{\alpha+1}$ for each $\alpha <\delta$.
    
    Fix $\alpha <\delta$. Now $t_{\alpha}$ belongs to $J\setminus I$, so by
    $(*)$, $(\aleph)$ or $(\beth)$
    holds. By Fact (D), it is enough to treat the case $(\aleph)$. So without loss of generality
    $\operatorname{Op} \big( (I,<)\upharpoonright \{ s\in I \colon (J,<)\models s<t_{\alpha}\}\big)=\kappa$.
    
    Let $$ I_{\alpha}^a=\{ t\in I_{\alpha}\colon t<t_{\alpha}\},$$
    $$I^b_{\alpha}=\{ t\in I_{\alpha +1} \colon t\in I_{\alpha}^a \vee tEt_{\alpha} \}, $$ $$I_{\alpha}^c=\{ t\in I_{\alpha} \colon t> t_{\alpha}\}.$$
     
    Note that $I_{\alpha}=I^a_{\alpha}+I^c_{\alpha}$ and
    $I_{\alpha+1}=I^b_{\alpha}+I^c_{\alpha}$. Recalling Fact (C), it is now enough to
    show that
    $I^a_{\alpha}\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq I^b_{\alpha}$. Identifying isomorphic orders and using $(\aleph)$,
    one has that $\underline\kappa$ is unbounded in $I_{\alpha}^a$ and $I_{\alpha}^b=I^a_{\alpha}+
    (I_{\alpha}^b\setminus I_{\alpha}^a)$ so by Fact (B), $I_{\alpha}^a\underset{\rm{nice}}  \subseteq I_{\alpha}^b$
    as required.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{X2.10}
    Suppose that $K$ is categorical in
    $\lambda > \chi$ (notice that $\lambda$ is not necessarily regular).  Then:
    
    (1) $K$ has a model $M$ of power $\lambda$ such that if  $N \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M$ and
    $\| N \| < \lambda$, then there
    exists $N'$ such that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(\alpha)$] $N \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N' \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M,$
        
        \item[$(\beta)$] $\| N' \| = \| N \| + \chi,$
        
        \item[$(\gamma)$] $N' \underset{\text{nice}}  \leq M.$
    \end{enumerate}
    
    (2) $K$ has a model $M$ of power $\lambda$ and an expansion $M^+$ of $M$ by at most $\chi$
    functions such that if $N^+ \subseteq M^+$, then $N^+ \upharpoonright \tau \underset{\text{nice}}  \leq M$.

title: Proof
body_md:
1) Let $\langle I, \langle A_i \colon  i \le \lambda \rangle \rangle$
    be as in Fact \ref{X2.7}. 
    Let $M = \operatorname{EM}(I)$.  Suppose that $N \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M,  \| N \| < \lambda$.
    Then there exists $J \subseteq I,
    |J| < \lambda$ such that $N \subseteq \operatorname{EM}(J)$ so by Fact \ref{X2.7} there exists $X \subseteq \lambda + 1$ such that $\lambda \in X,$ $\vert X \vert < \lambda$ and $J \subseteq \underset{i \in X} \cup A_i$. 
    
    Note that $\left| \underset{i \in X} \cup A_i \right| \le \vert X \vert \cdot \kappa < \lambda$.
    Now $N' = \operatorname{EM}(I \upharpoonright \underset{i \in X} \cup A_i)$
    is as required, since
    $I \upharpoonright \underset{ i \in X} \cup A_i \underset{\text{nice}}  \leq I$ and so by Theorem \ref{X2.5} 
    $\operatorname{EM}(I \upharpoonright \left( \bigcup_{i \in X} A_{i} \right)) \underset{\text{nice}}  \leq \operatorname{EM}(I)$.  This proves (1).
    
    (2) We expand $M = \operatorname{EM}(I)$ with skeleton $\langle a_{s} \colon s \in I \rangle$ as follows:

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] by all functions of $\operatorname{EM}'(I),$
        
        \item[(b)] by the unary functions $f_\ell(\ell<n)$ which are chosen as
        follows: we know that for each $b \in M$ there is $\sigma_b$ an $\tau_1$-term ($\tau_1$-the vocabulary of $\operatorname{EM}'(I)$) and $t(b,0) < t(b,1) < \ldots < t(b,n_{\sigma_b}-1)$ from $I$ such that $$b=\sigma_b(a_{t(b,0)}, a_{t(b,1)}, \dots, a_{t(b, n_{\sigma_{b}}-1)})$$
        
        (it is not unique, but we can choose one; really if we choose it with $n_b$ minimal it is almost unique). We let $$ f_\ell(b) =
        \begin{cases} a_{t((b,\ell))}, &\text{ if } \ell<n_{\sigma_b},\\
        b, &\text{ if } \ell\ge n_{\sigma_b}.\\ \end{cases}
        $$
        
        \item[(c)] by unary functions $g_\alpha$, $g^\alpha$ for $\alpha<\kappa$ such that
        \underbar{if} $t  < s$ are in $I$, $\alpha = \mathrm{otp}[(t,s)^*_I]$ then
        $g^\alpha(a_t)=a_s$, $\bigvee\limits_{\beta< \kappa}g_\beta(a_s)=a_t$
        (more formally $g^\alpha(a_{(i, \beta)})=a_{(i, \beta+\alpha)}$ and
        $g_\alpha(a_{(i, \beta)}) = a_{(i, \alpha)}$)
        in the other cases $g^\alpha(b)=b$, $g_\alpha(b)=b$.
        
        \item[(d)] by individual constants $c_\alpha=a_{(\lambda,\alpha)}$ for $\alpha<\kappa$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Call the expanded model $M^{+}$. Now suppose $N^+$ is a sub-model of $M^+$ and $N$ its $\tau$-reduct.
    Let $J\mathop=\limits^{\hbox{\rm def}}\{t\in I\colon a_t\in N\}$, now $J$ is a subset of $I$ of cardinality $\le||N||$ as for $t\not=s$ from $J$, $a_t\not= a_s$. Also if $b\in N$ by clause (b), $a_{t(b,\ell)}\in N$ hence $b\in \operatorname{EM}(J)$; on the other hand if $b\in \operatorname{EM}(J)$ then by clause (b) we have $b\in N$; so we can conclude $N=\operatorname{EM}(J)$. So far this holds for any linear suborder of $I$.
    
    By clause (c) $J=\bigcup\limits_{i\in X}A_i$ for some $X\subseteq \lambda+1$, and by clause (d), $\lambda \in X$.
    
    Now $\operatorname{EM}(J) \underset{\rm{nice}}{\leq} \operatorname{EM}(I) = M$ by Fact \ref{X2.7}.

\label{X3.6}
    Suppose that $\theta \in [\chi, \lambda)$ and  $\partial$ is a cardinal.
    
    (1) A model $M \in K_\theta$ is $\partial$-universal iff for every
    $N \in K_\partial$, there exists an $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-elementary embedding $f\colon  N \underset{\mathfrak{k}} \rightarrow M$. We say $M$ is universal iff $M$ is $\| M \|$-universal.
    
    (2) A model $M_2 \in K_{\theta}$ is $\partial$-universal over the model $M_1$ (and one writes $M_1 \underset{\partial-\rm{univ}} \preceq M_2$) \underline{iff} $M_1 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_2$ and whenever $M_1 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M'_2 \in K_{\partial}$, then there exists an $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-elementary embedding $f\colon  M'_2 \underset{\mathfrak{k}}  \rightarrow M_2$ such that $f \upharpoonright M_1$ is the identity.  (The embedding version runs:  there exists $h\colon  M_1 \underset{\mathfrak{k}} \rightarrow M_2$ and whenever $g \colon  M_1 \underset{\mathfrak{k}} \rightarrow M'_2 \in K_{ \partial }$, then there exists $f\colon  M'_2 \underset{\mathfrak{k}} \rightarrow M_2$ such that $f g = h$.) $M_2$ is universal over $M_1 \ (M_1 \underset{\text{univ}} \preceq M_2)$
    iff $M_2$ is $\|M_2 \|$-universal over $M_1$.
    
    (3) A model $M_2$ is $\partial$-universal over $M_1$ in $M$ \underline{iff} $M_1 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_2 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M$, $||M_1||\le\partial$ and whenever $M'_2 \in K_{\partial}$ and $M_1 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M'_2 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}}M$, then there exists an $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-elementary embedding $f\colon  M'_2 \underset{\mathfrak{k}} \rightarrow M_2$ such that $f \upharpoonright M_1$ is the identity.  $M_2$ is universal over $M_1$ in $M$ iff $M_2$ is $\| M_2 \|$-universal over $M_1$ in $M$.
    
    (4) $M_2$ is weakly $\partial$-universal over $M_1$ (written $M_1 \underset{\partial- \rm{wu}} \prec M_2$) \underline{iff} $M_1 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_2\in K_\partial$ and whenever $M_2 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M'_2 \in K_{\partial}$, then there exists an $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-elementary embedding $f\colon  M'_2 \underset{\mathfrak{k}}  \rightarrow M_2$ such that $f \upharpoonright M_1$ is the identity.  (The embedding version is:  there exists $h\colon  M_1 \underset{\mathfrak{k}}  \rightarrow M_2$ and whenever $g \colon  M_2 \underset{\mathfrak{k}} \rightarrow M'_2 \in K_{\partial}$, then there exists $f \colon  M'_2 \underset{\mathfrak{k}} \rightarrow M_2$ such that $h = f g h$ (written $h\colon  M_1 \underset{\partial-\rm{wu}} \rightarrow M_2$)). We say  $M_2$ is weakly universal over $M_1 (M_1 \underset{\rm{wu}} \preceq M_2)$ iff $M_2$ is $\|M_2 \|$-weakly universal over $M_1$.

\label{X4.2}

title: Proof
body_md:
ne proves (1), (2), and (3)
    simultaneously by induction on $\partial$.
    
    \underbar{Ad (1)}.  Choose a continuous $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-chain $\langle M_i \in K_\theta\colon  i < \partial \rangle$ of nice models by induction on $i$ as follows.  For $i = 0$, apply \ref{X3.11} to find a nice universal model $M_0 \in K_\theta$.  For $i = j +1$, note that $M_j$ is an a.b. by \ref{X3.5} (since $M_j$ is nice), hence by \ref{X3.10} there exists a nice model $M_i \in K_\theta, M_j \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_i, M_i$ universal over $M_j$.  For limit $i$, let $M_i = \underset{j < i} \cup M_j$.  Note that by the inductive hypothesis (3) on $\partial$ for $i < \partial$, since $M_i$ is $(\theta, i)$-saturated, $M_i$ is nice. Thus $M = \underset{i < \partial} \cup M_i$ is $(\theta, \partial)$-saturated (witnessed by $\langle M_i \colon  i < \partial \rangle$).  Note that $M$ is universal since $\langle M_i \colon  i < \partial \rangle$ is continuous and $M_0$ is universal.
    
    \underbar{Ad (2)}. Recall that each $M_{i}$ is an amalgamation base by $\ref{X2.1}.$  As $\partial$ is a limit ordinal
    standard back-and-forth argument shows that if $M$ and $N$ are $(\theta, \partial)$-saturated models, then $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic.
    
    \underbar{Ad (3)}.  By the uniqueness (i.e. by Ad(2)) it suffices to prove that some $(\theta, \partial)$-saturated model is nice. Suppose that $M$ is $(\theta, \partial)$-saturated. We'll show that $M$ is nice.
    
    If $ \mathrm{cf}(\partial) < \partial$, then $M$ is also ($\theta$, $\mathrm{cf}(\partial$))-saturated and hence by the inductive hypothesis (3) on $\partial$ for cf$(\partial), M$ is nice. So we'll assume that cf$(\partial) = \partial$.  Choose a continuous $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-chain $\langle M_i \in K_\theta \colon  i < \theta^+ \rangle$ such that: $M_0$ is nice and universal (possible by \ref{X3.11}); if $M_i$ is nice, then $M_{i +1} \in K_\theta$ is nice and universal over $M_i$ (possible by \ref{X3.5} and \ref{X3.10}); if $M_i$ is not nice (so necessarily $i$ is a limit ordinal), then $M_{i +1} \in K_\theta, M_i \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_{i +1}$ and $M_i \underset{\text{nice}}  \nleq M_{i +1}$. By \ref{X3.1} and \ref{X1.10} there is a club $C$ of $\theta^+$ such that if $i \in C$, then $M_i \underset{\text{nice}}  \leq M_{i +1}$.  So by the choice of $\langle M_i \colon  i < \theta^+ \rangle$, if $i \in C$, then $M_i$ is nice.  Choose $i \in C, i = \sup (i \cap C)$, $\mathrm{cf}(i) = \partial$. It suffices to show that $M_i$ is $(\theta, \partial)$-saturated (for then by (2) $M_i$ is isomorphic to $M$ and so $M$ is nice). Choose a continuous increasing sequence $\langle \alpha_\zeta\colon  \zeta < \partial \rangle \subseteq C$ such that $i = \bigcup \{ \alpha_{\zeta}\colon  \zeta < \partial \}$ (recall that $i = \sup (i \cap C)$,  $\mathrm{cf}(i) = \partial$).  Now $M_i = \underset{\zeta < \partial} \cup M_{\alpha_\zeta}$.  Of course $M_{\alpha_0}$ is universal (since $M_0$ is universal and $M_0 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_{\alpha_0}$), $M_{\alpha_{\zeta+1}}$ is universal over $M_{\alpha_\zeta}$ since $M_{\alpha_\zeta +1}$ is universal over $M_{\alpha_\zeta}$ and $M_{\alpha_\zeta} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_{\alpha_\zeta +1} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_{\alpha_{\zeta + 1}}$. Also $M_{\alpha_\zeta}$ is nice for each $\zeta < \partial$ since $\alpha_\zeta \in C$.  Hence $M_i$ is $(\theta, \partial)$-saturated, recall that $M_{i}$ is nice because $i \in C,$ so we are done.

By \ref{X3.1} there exists a club $C_2 \subseteq C_{1}$ of $\theta^+$ such that for every $\delta\in C_2$, $N\upharpoonright \delta \underset{\rm{nice}}{\leq} N$. Since $\{ |N_i|  \colon i < \theta^+ \}$ is a continuous increasing sequence of subsets of $\theta^+$, it follows that $C_3=\{ \delta<\theta^+  \colon \delta \subseteq |N_{\delta}|\}$ is a club of $\theta^+$. Hence there is a club $C_4$ of $\theta^+$ such that $C_4\subseteq C_1\cap C_2 \cap C_3\cap [\theta, \theta^+)$. Note that for $\delta\in C_4$ one has $N\upharpoonright \delta \underset{\rm{nice}} \leq N$, $|N\upharpoonright \delta|= \delta \subseteq |N_{\delta}|$ and $N_{\delta}  \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N$, so that $N\upharpoonright \delta \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N_{\delta} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N$ and so by \ref{X1.10} $N\upharpoonright \delta \underset{\rm{nice}} \leq N_\delta$. $\langle N_{\delta} \colon \delta\in C_4\rangle$ is a continuous increasing $\prec_{\mathfrak{k}}$-chain, $N_{\delta}\in K_{\theta^+}$ and $N\upharpoonright \delta\in K_{\theta}$.

But $N_{\delta+1}$ is universal over $N_{\delta}$ (by (ii)), so $A_{\delta}$ can be $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-elementarily embedded into $N_{\delta+1}$ over $N_{\delta}$ (say by $g_{\delta}$), hence $B_{\delta}$ can be $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-elementarily embedded into $N$ (using $g_{\delta}f_{\delta}$).]

[For $\alpha \in C_4$, let $E_{\alpha}=(\sup |B_{\alpha}|, \theta^+)\cap C_4$, let $E_{\alpha}=\theta^+$ for $\alpha\not\in C_4$ and let $E$ be the diagonal intersection of $\langle E_{\alpha} \colon  \alpha <\theta^+\rangle$, i.e. $E=\{ \delta<\theta^+\colon (\forall \alpha <\delta)(\delta\in E_{\alpha})\}$. Note that $E$ is a club of

    Thus $\langle N\upharpoonright\delta\colon \delta\in C_5\rangle$ is a continuous $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-chain of nice models, each of power $\theta$. If $\delta_1\in C_5$ and $\delta_2=\min(C_5\setminus (\delta_1+1))$, then
    $N\upharpoonright \delta_1 \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} B_{\delta_1} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N\upharpoonright \delta_2$. Hence $N\upharpoonright \delta_2$ is universal over $N\upharpoonright\delta_1$ (since $B_{\delta_1}$ is universal over

title: Proof
body_md:
et $\theta = \sup(\bar{\theta}).$ By \ref{X4.9}(1) and the uniqueness of $\overline\theta$-saturated models \ref{X4.9}(2), without loss of generality one may assume that $\lg(\overline\theta) = \mathrm{cf}(\sup (\overline\theta)) = \mathrm{cf}(\theta)$. Now, by \ref{X4.6}, we know $(\mathrm{cf}(\theta))^+<\theta \ (= \sup(\bar{\theta}))$, so by \cite[\ref{X1.5} + Fact \ref{X1.2}(1)]{Sh:420} 
    there exists $\langle S, \langle C_{\alpha} 
 \colon \alpha \in S\rangle\rangle$ such that: 
    
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[{$(\alpha)$}] $S\subseteq \theta^+$ is a set of ordinals; $ 0 \notin S,$
        
        \item[{$(\beta)$}] $S_1=\{ \alpha\in S\colon  \mathrm{cf}(\alpha)= \mathrm{cf} (\theta)\}$ is a stationary subset of $\theta^+,$
        
        \item[{$(\gamma)$}] if $\alpha \in S$ 
        then $\alpha=\sup (C_{\alpha})$ and, if $\alpha\in S \setminus S_{1}$ then $\rm{otp}(C_{\alpha}) < \mathrm{cf} (\theta),$
    
        \item[{$(\delta)$}] if $\beta \in C_{\alpha}$, then $\beta \in S$ and $C_{\beta}=C_{\alpha}\cap \beta,$
    
        \item[{$(\epsilon)$}] $C_{\alpha}$ is a set of successor ordinals.
    \end{itemize}
    
    [Note that the existence of $\langle S,\langle C_{\alpha} \colon \alpha \in S\rangle\rangle$
    is provable in ZFC.] 
    
    Without loss of generality $S\setminus S_1=\cup\{C_\alpha \colon \alpha\in S_1\}$.
    We shall construct the required model by induction, using $\langle  C_{\alpha} \colon \alpha \in S\rangle$.  Remember $\bar \theta=\langle \theta_\zeta\colon  \zeta< \mathrm{cf}(\theta)\rangle$.
    Let us start by defining by induction on $\alpha<\theta^+$ the following entities: $M_{\alpha}$, $M_{\alpha, \xi}$ (for $\alpha<\theta^+$, $\xi < \mathrm{cf}(\theta))$, and $N_\alpha$ (only when $\alpha\in\bigcup\limits_{\beta\in S}C_\beta$)  such that:
    
    \item{(A1)} $M_{\alpha} \in K_{\theta}$,
    
    \item{(A2)} $\langle M_{\alpha} \colon  \alpha < \theta^+\rangle$ is a continuous increasing $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-chain of models,
    
    \item{(A3)} $M_{\alpha +1}$ is nice, and if $M_{\alpha}$ is not nice, then $M_{\alpha} {\underset  {\text{nice}}  {\not\nleq}}  M_{\alpha+1},$
    
    \item{(A4)} $M_{\alpha} \not= M_{\alpha+1},$
    
    \item{(A5)} $M_{\alpha+1}$ is weakly universal over $M_{\alpha},$
    
    \item{(B1)} $M_{\alpha}=\bigcup\limits_{\xi<\mathrm{cf}(\theta)}M_{\alpha, \xi}$, $||M_{\alpha, \xi}||=\theta_{\xi},$

    \item{(B2)} if $\alpha \in S_1 \; , \; \beta \in C_{\alpha} \; , \; \gamma\in C_{\alpha} \; , \; \beta < \gamma$, then:

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)]   $N_{\beta} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_{\beta}$,

        \item[(b)] $||N_{\beta}||=\theta_{\mathrm{otp}(C_{\beta})}$,

        \item[(c)] $(\forall \xi < \mathrm{otp}(C_{\beta}))(M_{\beta, \xi} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N_{\gamma}),$

        \item[(d)] $N_{\beta}$ is nice,

        \item[(e)] $N_{\gamma}$ is $\theta_{\mathrm{otp}(C_{\gamma})}$-universal over $N_{\beta}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    There are now two tasks at hand.
    First of all, we shall explain how to construct these entities (THE CONSTRUCTION, below).
    Then we shall use them to build a nice $\overline\theta$-saturated  model (PROVING  $\Pr(\overline\theta)$, below). \relax From the uniqueness of $\overline\theta$-saturated models it will
    thus follow that $\Pr(\overline\theta)$ holds.

    \underline{THE CONSTRUCTION}: we consider several cases: 
    
    \underline{Case (i)}: $\beta=0$. Choose $M_0\in K_{\theta}$ and $\langle M_{0, \xi} \in K_{\theta} \colon  \xi< \mathrm{cf}(\theta) \rangle$
    with $M_0=\bigcup\limits_{\xi<\mathrm{cf}(\theta)}M_{0, \xi}$ using Fact \ref{X1.2}. There is no need to define $N_0$ since $0\not\in C_{\alpha}$.
    
    Case (ii): $\beta$ is a limit ordinal. Let $M_{\beta}=\bigcup\limits_{\gamma<\beta}M_{\gamma}$
    and choose $\langle M_{\beta, \xi} \colon  \xi < \mathrm{cf}(\theta)\rangle$ using Fact \ref{X1.2}. Again there's no call
    to define $N_{\beta}$ since $C_{\alpha}$ is always a set of successor ordinals.
    
    Case (iii): $\beta$ is a successor ordinal, $\beta=\gamma+1$. Choose $M'_\gamma\in K_\theta$ such that $M_\gamma \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M'_{\gamma}$ and if possible $M_\gamma \underset{\text{nice}}  {\nleq} M'_\gamma$; without loss of generality $M'_\gamma$ is weakly universal over $M_\gamma$. If $\beta\not\in S$, then define things as above, taking into account (A3).  The definitions of $M_{\beta}$, $M_{\beta, \xi}$ present no special difficulties. Now suppose that $\beta\in S$. The problematic entity to define is $N_{\beta}$.

    If $C_{\beta}=\emptyset$, choose for $N_{\beta}$ any nice sub-model (of power $\theta_{0}$) of
    $M_{\gamma}$.

    If $C_{\beta}\not=\emptyset$, then first define $N^-_{\beta}=\bigcup\limits_{\gamma\in C_{\beta}}N_{\gamma}$. Note that $N^-_{\beta}$ is nice. [If $C_{\beta}$ has a last element $\beta'$, then $N^-_{\beta}=N_{\beta'}$ which is nice; if $C_{\beta}$ has no last element, then $N^-_{\beta}=\bigcup\limits_{\gamma\in C_{\beta}}N_{\gamma}$ is $\overline\theta\upharpoonright \mathrm{otp}(C_{\beta})$-saturated, and, by the hypothesis of the theorem, $\Pr(\overline\theta\upharpoonright \mathrm{otp}(C_{\beta}))$, so $N^-_{\beta}$ is nice.] Also $N^-_\beta \preceq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_\gamma$. If $\rm{otp}(C_\beta)$ is a limit ordinal we let $N_\beta=N^-_\beta$ and $M_\beta= M^\prime_\gamma$, so we have finished, so assume $\mathrm{otp}(C_\beta)$ is a successor ordinal. To complete the definition of $N_{\beta}$, one requires a Lemma (the proof of which is similar to \ref{X3.9}, \ref{X3.10}):
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[{$(\ast)$}] if $A\subseteq M\in K_{\theta}$, $|A|\le \theta_j<\theta$, then there exist a nice $M^+\in K_{\theta}$, $M \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M^+$, and nice models $N^*$, $N^+\in K_{\theta_j}$, $A \subseteq N^* \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N^+ \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M^+$ and $N^+$ is universal over $N^*$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Why is this enough? Use the Lemma with $M=M'_{\beta}$ and $A=N^-_{\beta}\cup \bigcup\limits_{\scriptstyle \xi< \mathrm{otp}(C_{\beta}) \atop \scriptstyle \gamma\in C_{\beta}}M_{\gamma, \xi}$  to find $N^*$, $N^+$, $M^+$ and choose $N^+$, $M^+$ as $N_\beta$, $M_\beta$ respectively. 
    
    Now, why $(*)$ holds? The proof of $(\ast)$ is easy as $M'_\beta$ is nice.
    
    \underline{PROVING Pr$(\overline\theta)$}:

    For $\alpha \in S_1$, consider $\langle N_{\beta} \colon  \beta \in C_{\alpha}\rangle$. For $\beta,\gamma\in C_{\alpha}, \beta<\gamma$,  one has by (B2)(c) $\bigcup\limits_{\xi < \mathrm{otp} (C_{\beta})}M_{\beta, \xi} \subseteq N_{\gamma}$. Therefore $M_{\beta} \subseteq \bigcup\limits_{\gamma\in C_{\alpha}}N_{\gamma}.$ $(M_\beta=\bigcup\limits_{\xi<\mathrm{cf}(\theta)}M_{\beta, \xi}=\bigcup\limits_{\xi<\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)} M_{\beta, \xi} $  (since $\alpha\in S_1)$; for $\xi <\mathrm{cf}(\alpha)$, choose $\gamma \in C_{\alpha}$,
    $\xi<\gamma, \beta<\gamma$; so $M_{\beta, \xi}\subseteq N_{\gamma}$ and $M_{\beta}\subseteq \bigcup\limits_{\gamma\in C_{\alpha}}N_{\gamma})$.

    Thus for every $\beta\in C_{\alpha}$,
    $M_{\beta}\subseteq \bigcup\limits_{\gamma\in C_{\alpha}}N_{\gamma}$ hence $M_\alpha = \bigcup\limits_{\beta\in C_\alpha} M_\beta \subseteq \bigcup\limits_{\gamma\in C_\alpha} N_\gamma$ (remember $\alpha = \sup (C_\alpha)$ as $\alpha \in S_1$). If $\gamma\in C_{\alpha}$, then $N_{\gamma} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} M_{\gamma}$ (by (B2)(a)), and so $\bigcup\limits_{\gamma\in C_{\alpha}}N_{\gamma} \subseteq \bigcup\limits_{\beta\in C_{\alpha}}
    M_{\beta}=M_{\alpha}$ by continuity.
    So $M_\alpha = \bigcup\limits_{\beta\in C_\alpha} N_\beta$ hence $\langle N_\beta\colon  \beta\in C_\alpha\rangle$ exemplifies $M_\alpha$ is
    $\bar \theta$-saturated (remember $\Pr(\bar \theta \upharpoonright \delta)$ for every limit $\delta< \rm{lg}(\bar \theta)$). So $M_{\alpha}$ is $\overline\theta$-saturated for every $\alpha\in S_1$. In other words $\{\alpha<\theta^+ \colon  M_{\alpha}$ is $\overline\theta$-saturated$\} \supseteq S_1$ and is stationary, so, applying \ref{X3.1}, there exists
    $\alpha<\theta^+$ such that $M_{\alpha}$ is $\overline\theta$-saturated and $M_{\alpha}\underset{\rm{nice}} \leq \bigcup\limits_{\beta<\theta^+}M_{\beta}$.  Hence by \ref{X1.10} $M_{\alpha} \underset{\rm{nice}}{\leq} M_{\alpha+1}$ and so, since $M_{\alpha+1}$ is nice (A3), $M_{\alpha}$ is nice (by \ref{X3.12}).
    
    We conclude that Pr$(\overline\theta)$ holds.

body_md:
M \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} \underset{i < \mathrm{cf}(\mu)}  \cup M_i  \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} \underset{i < \mathrm{cf}(\mu)}  \cup L^0_i = L \in K_\mu$. Suppose that $A \subseteq |L|$.  If $|A| = \mu$, then necessarily $\mu<\lambda$ and we take $N = L$.  So without loss of generality, $|A| < \mu$.  If $\mu = \mathrm{cf}(\mu)$ or $|A| < \mathrm{cf}(\mu)$, then there is $i < \mathrm{cf}(\mu)$ such that $A \subseteq L^1_i$ and, by $(\gamma), (\ast)_{L^1_i}$ holds, so there is $N \in K_{\kappa + \mathrm{LST}(\mathfrak{k}) + |A|}, A \subseteq N \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} L^1_i, N$ is nice and $N \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} L$ as required.  So suppose that $\mathrm{cf}(\mu) \le |A| < \mu$.  Choose by induction on $i < \mathrm{cf}(\mu)$ models $N^0_i, N^1_i, N^2_i$ in that order such that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(\alpha)$] $N_{i}^{0} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N_{i}^{1} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N_{i}^{2},$
        
        \item[$(\beta)$] $N_{i}^{2} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N_{i+1}^{0},$
        
        \item[$(\gamma)$] $A \cap L_{i}^{0} \subseteq N_{i}^{0} \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} L_{i}^{0},$  
        
        \item[$(\delta)$] $N^1_i \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} L^1_i$ and $ N^1_i$ is nice,
        
        \item[$(\varepsilon)$] $N^2_i \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} L^2_i, N^2_i$  is nice and  universal over $N^1_i,$
        
        \item[$(\zeta)$] $N^0_i, N^1_i, N^2_i$ have power at most $\min\{\chi + |A|, \mu_i\}$.
    \end{enumerate}

    For $i =0$, apply Fact \ref{X1.2} for $A \cap L^0_0, L^0_0$; for $i = j +1$, apply Fact \ref{X1.2} to find $N^0_i \in K_{\mu_i}, (A \cap L^0_i) \cup N^2_j \subset N^0_i \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} L^0_i$ (in particular $N^2_j \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N^0_i)$; for limit $i, N^0_i = \underset{j < i} \cup N^0_j$.  To choose $N^1_i$, use $(\ast)_{L^1_i}$ for the set $A_i = N^0_i$ to find a nice $N^1_i \in K_{\le \chi + |A|}, N^0_i \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} N^1_i \leq_{\mathfrak{k}} L^1_i$. Note that $\| N^1_i \| \le \mu_i$.  Finally to choose $N^2_i$ note that by Lemma \ref{X3.9} the model $N^1_i$ has a nice extension $N^+_i$ (of power $\| N^1_i \|$) weakly universal over $N^1_i$.  Now $N^1_i$ is nice, hence $N_{i}^{+}$ is universal over $N^1_i$ (by \ref{X3.6}A(5)) and by  Lemma \ref{X2.1} there is an amalgam $N_i$ of $N^+_i, L^1_i$ over $N^1_i$ such that $\| N_i \| \le \mu_i$.  Since $L^2_i$ is universal over $L^1_i$ one can find an $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-elementary sub-model $N^2_i$ of $L^2_i$ isomorphic to $N_i$. Let $N_i$ be $N_i^0$ if $i$ is a limit, $N_i^1$ otherwise; prove by induction on $i$ that $N_i$ is nice (by Theorem \ref{X4.2}).
    
    Now $\underset{i < \mathrm{cf}(\mu)}  \cup N^0_i$ is an $\leq_{\mathfrak{k}}$-elementary sub-model of $L$ of power at most $\kappa + |T| + |A|$, including $A$ (by $(\gamma)$) and $\underset{i < \mathrm{cf}(\mu)}  \cup N^0_i$ is $(\chi + |A|, \mathrm{cf}(\mu))$-saturated, hence (by 
    Theorem \ref{X4.2}) nice, as required.
